title: Satsang, in person
hook: finding a room in your city (verified hosts only)

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan, the call and the answer. Your line was call, answer. Did you listen all the way to the end before you answered someone? Day one hundred and thirty-eight.

Look at this week. It opened at the temple steps: mandir, shoes off. Then darshan, seeing and being seen. Pradakshina, walking around. The pujari, who holds the form. Bhajan, loud. Kirtan, call and answer. Every one of those days had something in common: other people. You can light a lamp alone. You can't really do a kirtan alone. And there's a word you learned way back on day twenty, in the first camp, for exactly this. Back then it was an idea. Today, it's an address, a time, and a door you actually walk through. Today: satsang, in person.
screen: `A WEEK OF OTHER PEOPLE.` → `YOU CAN'T DO KIRTAN ALONE.` → `TODAY: SATSANG, IN PERSON.`

segments.voice: Satsang joins two words. Sat means true, real, good, what actually is. Sang means company, being together. So satsang is the company of the true, or good company, and your line from day twenty still holds: good company changes you. A satsang can be many things. A group in a temple hall on a Sunday. A few families in a living room, reading a chapter of the Gita. A student group on a campus. A weekly bhajan evening. Most follow a similar shape: some singing, a reading or a short talk, maybe questions, a few minutes of silence, prasad, and, almost always, tea afterward, which is where people become friends. So how do you find a good room? Start with what's established and public. Ask at a local temple; most have a notice board or a front desk. Ask a Hindu friend or coworker where their family goes. Look for groups that meet in open places and have been around for years. And a few honest signs to walk away: a group that pressures you to come back, asks for large sums of money, wants to cut you off from family or friends, or says only its teacher can be trusted. Good company doesn't grab. It welcomes, and lets you leave. You won't love every room. The first may feel awkward: you won't know the songs or when to stand. That's normal. Sit in the back, sing what you can, stay for the tea. Everything you've practiced this week, the shoes, the bow, the call and answer, was preparation for this.
screen: `SAT + SANG: THE COMPANY OF THE TRUE.` · `SINGING, READING, SILENCE, TEA.` · `START ESTABLISHED AND PUBLIC.` · `GOOD COMPANY DOESN'T GRAB.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Think of one place near you where people might gather like this: a temple, a community center, a campus, a friend's family. If you don't know any, picture yourself asking one person who might. Now choose one, just one, to try in the next month. Picture the evening: you arrive, shoes off, you find a spot at the back. Someone smiles and passes you a lyric sheet. You sing the parts you can. Afterward, someone hands you a cup of tea. The bell holds the time.
Satsang. The company of the true: people gathering to sing, read, sit in silence and share tea, and the good company that changes you. Today's word.

Your line: go. This week, find out one real time and place for a gathering near you, and put it in your calendar. That's the week. Tomorrow, the festivals begin with Diwali. Day one hundred and thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Hindus attend satsangs, regular gatherings at temples, homes or community halls that usually include devotional singing, a reading or talk, silence and prasad, followed by tea and conversation.

original.note: Sanskrit satsaṅga: company with the true or the good. Often written सत्संग.

trapdoor: what you thought: a spiritual meetup.
what it means: the company of the true: people gathering to sing, read and sit together, where good company changes you.

what a scholar hears: sat (being, truth) + saṅga (association); the value of satsanga is praised across bhakti and Vedanta literature, including Shankara's Bhaja Govindam, which traces a chain from good company to liberation.

sources.ref: Bhaja Govindam (attributed to Shankara), verse 9: good company leads to non-attachment, clarity and liberation
